opus-5.5.text:
I think my basic picture is that a lot of the remaining progress is going to come from just continuing to do the boring things: making models bigger, training them on more data, and doing a lot of fairly unglamorous engineering to make them work well in practice. I don't think we're in a world where we're waiting on some single conceptual breakthrough. I'm uncertain about that, but if you look at the trend, scaling has kept delivering pretty steady qualitative improvements, and I don't see strong evidence that it's about to stop.

That said, I don't think raw scale alone gets you to a system that can just walk in and do a human job. There's a big gap between "this model can answer questions or write code in a chat window" and "this system can be handed a messy, open-ended task, work on it for days, recover from mistakes, and coordinate with other people." Closing that gap is partly about scale making the underlying model smarter and more reliable, but a lot of it is engineering. You need good ways to fine-tune models for the specific tasks you care about, to give them tools and memory, to let them act over long horizons, and to get feedback on whether they're actually doing a good job. That last piece is really important. For many jobs, the hard part is that it's expensive to evaluate whether the work is good, so a lot of effort goes into building training signals and oversight that let you push performance up on things humans care about.

So if I'm trying to forecast, I imagine a few more orders of magnitude of effective compute, partly from hardware and spending and partly from algorithmic improvements, combined with years of iterative work integrating these systems into real workflows. My guess is that the combination makes it fairly plausible we see systems that can do a large fraction of cognitive work within something like a decade or two, with maybe a meaningful chance it happens sooner. I'd put wide error bars on that. It could turn out that some capabilities, like long-horizon planning or really robust reliability, are much harder than they look and need ideas we don't have yet. But my default is that scaling plus a lot of engineering is a credible path, and I think we should be taking that possibility seriously, including from a safety perspective, because the transition could happen faster than people's intuitions suggest.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects continued scaling and gives a broad timeline, but does not predict that scaling will be much faster in the next four or five years than afterward.

r002.rationale: The candidate identifies engineering work—such as fine-tuning, tools, memory, long-horizon action, feedback, and workflow integration—as contributing to progress toward systems that can do human jobs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I expect a lot of the remaining distance to be closed by things that look pretty boring from the outside. If you look at how far we've come over the last several years, a big chunk of it is just: more compute, more data, and a lot of engineering effort to actually make those things usable. And I don't see a strong reason to think that stops working anytime soon.

The way I'd break it down is something like this. There's a question of what the raw capability of the underlying model is, and scaling is clearly still driving that. Loss keeps going down as you add compute, and the loss improvements keep translating into things people care about, even if the mapping is noisy. So I think if you just kept doing what the labs are doing, you'd continue to see models that are better at reasoning, better at following long chains of instructions, better at not making the kind of dumb mistakes that currently make them annoying to work with.

But then there's a second question, which is: how much of the gap between "a model that's impressive in a demo" and "a model that can actually replace a human in a job" is about the model, versus about everything around it? And I think a surprisingly large fraction is the latter. Humans doing jobs have memory across days and weeks, they have tools, they get feedback and correct themselves, they know when to ask for help, they operate in an institutional context that's been built around them. Right now when you drop a language model into a job, almost none of that scaffolding exists for it. Building that out is mostly engineering. It's not glamorous, but it's the kind of thing where I expect a lot of steady progress, because the incentives are enormous and there's no fundamental obstacle.

So my picture is that scaling raises the ceiling, and engineering work is what lets you actually reach the ceiling in practice. And I think both of those matter a lot. If you froze model quality today and just spent five years on the surrounding infrastructure, I think you'd automate a lot more work than people expect. And if you froze the infrastructure and just scaled, you'd also see a lot of progress, because better models need less hand-holding.

The thing I'm more uncertain about is whether there are specific capabilities that neither of those get you, where you need some kind of qualitative insight. Historically people have guessed there would be such things, and the guesses have mostly been wrong, so I've updated toward thinking the remaining steps are less mysterious than they look. But I wouldn't put that at a hundred percent. I'd say my median expectation is that the path from here to systems that can do most human jobs is dominated by scaling and engineering, with maybe a few places where some new idea makes things easier or faster, rather than being a hard requirement.

And I guess the uncomfortable corollary is that if that's right, then the timeline is pretty much set by how fast people are willing to invest, not by when someone has a clever idea. Which is part of why I spend so much of my time worrying about whether we're ready for what happens when that investment pays off.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects scaling to keep driving progress, but does not predict that scaling will be much faster over the next four or five years than afterward.

r002.rationale: The candidate says engineering work to build the tools, memory, feedback, and other scaffolding around models can close much of the gap to doing human jobs.

astra-6.text:
I think additional scaling and engineering work are likely to get us a very long way. I don’t know whether you can take the exact recipe we have now, turn up the compute, and get a system that can do essentially every human job. But I also don’t see a strong reason to expect some fundamental obstacle that requires a completely different approach.

There’s a distinction between a system being able to do an impressive task once and being able to reliably do someone’s job. A job involves doing lots of things, noticing when something has gone wrong, asking for clarification, and keeping track of what you’re trying to accomplish over a long period. Current systems have weaknesses there. Some of those weaknesses may improve with scale, and some may require training on those kinds of tasks or building better infrastructure around the model.

So the question isn’t just, ‘How much smarter does the next model get?’ It’s also, ‘How much work does it take to turn that intelligence into useful labor?’ You could have substantial economic progress from figuring out how to use capabilities that are already present. And as models become more useful for that engineering work themselves, that could accelerate the process. I’m uncertain about the timing, but I wouldn’t assume that we need a major conceptual breakthrough before these systems can do a very large fraction of human work.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling and engineering could get AI a long way and expresses uncertainty about timing, but it does not predict that scaling will be much faster in the next four or five years than afterward.

r002.rationale: It identifies engineering work and better infrastructure around models as ways to turn existing capabilities into useful labor and help systems perform jobs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think additional scaling and engineering can get us a very long way. We have systems that can already do parts of a lot of jobs, and there are fairly straightforward ways to make them more useful: make them more reliable, give them tools, let them work on a task for longer, and train them on the kinds of problems you actually want them to solve.

The big uncertainty is how much is missing beyond that. Doing well on a short, well-specified task is different from taking responsibility for a project where you have to figure out what matters, notice when something has gone wrong, and recover. You can imagine those capabilities improving continuously as models get better, or you can imagine running into problems that require more substantial changes.

My guess is that scaling and engineering will account for a large fraction of the remaining progress. That doesn’t mean you can confidently extrapolate a date. It means I don’t see a compelling reason to expect some particular human capability to remain out of reach of that process.

r001.rationale: It predicts scaling and engineering will account for much of the remaining progress, but gives no comparison between the next four or five years and later years.

r002.rationale: It identifies engineering improvements—such as reliability, tools, longer task work, and relevant training—as ways to make AI systems more useful for jobs.
